shanti.1: Om. O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good; O you who are worthy of worship, may we see with our eyes what is good. With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span of life the gods have set. May Indra of great fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, who knows all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel no one can harm, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being. Om, peace, peace, peace.

The śānti pāṭha of the Upaniṣads of the Atharvaveda (Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya), from the Ṛgveda (1.89.8 and 1.89.6). Tārkṣya is Garuḍa; ariṣṭanemi, “whose wheel-rim is unharmed”, is also read “who wards off harm”. Peace is said three times, for freedom from the troubles that come from oneself, from other beings and from the powers of nature.
1.1.1: Om. Brahmā, the foremost of the gods, came into being, the maker of the universe and the protector of the world. He taught the knowledge of Brahman (the Absolute), the ground of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son. ॥1.1.1॥
Śaṅkara also takes prathamaḥ as first in time, born before the other gods.
1.1.2: The knowledge that Brahmā taught to Atharvan, that knowledge of Brahman Atharvan told of old to Aṅgir. Aṅgir taught it to Satyavāha of the line of Bharadvāja, and Satyavāha the Bhāradvāja taught it, handed down from teacher to pupil, to Aṅgiras. ॥1.1.2॥
Śaṅkara also takes parāvarā as the knowledge that covers every subject of knowledge, the higher and the lower.
1.1.3: Śaunaka, the great householder, having duly approached Aṅgiras, asked: Venerable sir, what is it that, once known, makes all this known? ॥1.1.3॥
1.1.4: Aṅgiras said to him: Two kinds of knowledge are to be known, as the knowers of Brahman say: the higher and the lower. ॥1.1.4॥
1.1.5: Of these, the lower is the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda and the Atharvaveda, phonetics, the ritual code, grammar, etymology, metre and astronomy. And the higher is that by which the Imperishable (akṣara) is attained. ॥1.1.5॥
1.1.6: That which cannot be seen or grasped, which has no origin and no colour, which has neither eyes nor ears, neither hands nor feet; which is eternal, taking many forms, present everywhere and exceedingly subtle: that is the Imperishable, which the wise see everywhere as the source of all beings. ॥1.1.6॥
1.1.7: As a spider sends out its thread and draws it in, as plants spring up on the earth, as hair of the head and body comes from a living man, so here the universe arises from the Imperishable. ॥1.1.7॥
1.1.8: Through tapas (heat, austerity) Brahman swells; from it food is born. From food come prāṇa (the life-breath), mind, the true and the worlds, and in works the immortal (their fruit). ॥1.1.8॥

Śaṅkara takes tapas here as knowledge (the next mantra: whose tapas is made of knowledge), Brahman's swelling as its turning towards creation, food as the unmanifest, prāṇa as Hiraṇyagarbha and the true as the five elements.
1.1.9: He who is all-knowing and knows each thing, whose tapas is made of knowledge: from him are born this Brahman, name, form and food. ॥1.1.9॥
Śaṅkara takes this Brahman as Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahman as effect; sarvajña as knowing all in general and sarvavit as knowing each thing in particular.
1.1.iti: Thus ends the first khaṇḍa (section) of the first Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
1.2.1: This is the truth: the works that the seers saw in the mantras are spread out in many forms in the three Vedas. Perform them always, you who desire their true fruit; this is your path to the world your own good works win. ॥1.2.1॥
Śaṅkara takes tretāyām as in the three Vedas (the work of the hotṛ, adhvaryu and udgātṛ priests), or as in the Tretā age, when these rites were mostly performed.
1.2.2: When the flame flickers, once the fire that carries the offerings is well kindled, then one should cast the oblations between the two portions of ghee (the ājyabhāgas). ॥1.2.2॥
1.2.3: If one's agnihotra (the daily fire offering) lacks the new-moon and full-moon rites, lacks the four-monthly rites and the offering of first fruits, and is without guests honoured, is not offered, lacks the offering to all the gods, or is offered without rule — it destroys his worlds, all seven of them. ॥1.2.3॥
Śaṅkara takes the seven worlds as the seven from bhūḥ up to satya, which rightly done rites would win, or as father, grandfather, great-grandfather, son, grandson, great-grandson and oneself.
1.2.4: Kālī the black, Karālī the fearsome and Manojavā, swift as thought, Sulohitā, deep red, and she who is Sudhūmravarṇā, the colour of smoke, Sphuliṅginī, full of sparks, and the goddess Viśvarucī, bright in every form: these are the seven flickering tongues of fire. ॥1.2.4॥
1.2.5: He who performs the rites in these shining flames at their proper time, him these oblations take up and, as the rays of the sun, lead to where the one lord of the gods (Indra) dwells. ॥1.2.5॥
1.2.6: Come, come, they call to him, and the radiant oblations carry the sacrificer on the rays of the sun, speaking pleasant words and honouring him: This is your holy world of Brahmā, won by your good works. ॥1.2.6॥
Śaṅkara takes the world of Brahmā here to mean heaven, the fruit of works.
1.2.7: Perishable indeed and unsteady are these forms of sacrifice, the eighteen, on whom the lower work is said to rest. The deluded who hail this as the highest good go to old age and death again and again. ॥1.2.7॥
Śaṅkara takes the eighteen as the sixteen priests, the sacrificer and his wife.
Plava is also read as a raft: these sacrifices are unsteady rafts.
1.2.8: Dwelling in the midst of ignorance, wise in their own eyes and thinking themselves learned, the deluded wander about, struck again and again, like the blind led by one who is blind. ॥1.2.8॥
1.2.9: Living in ignorance in many ways, the childish think: We have reached our goal. Because those given to works do not know the truth, out of attachment, they fall, stricken, when the worlds their merit won are spent. ॥1.2.9॥
1.2.10: Thinking sacrifices and works of public good the highest, the utterly deluded know no other good. Having enjoyed their fruit on the height of heaven, won by good works, they enter this world, or one still lower. ॥1.2.10॥
1.2.11: But those who practise tapas and faith, dwelling in the forest, at peace, learned, living on alms, go, free of stain, through the door of the sun to where that immortal Person (puruṣa) is, whose nature never decays. ॥1.2.11॥
Śaṅkara takes this immortal Person as Hiraṇyagarbha, who lasts as long as the world does; this path too is a fruit of the lower knowledge.
1.2.12: Having examined the worlds that works win, a brāhmaṇa should come to dispassion: here nothing is unmade, so what use is what is done? To know that, let him go only to a teacher, fuel in hand, to one versed in the Veda and established in Brahman. ॥1.2.12॥
1.2.13: To the pupil who has duly approached him, whose mind is at peace and who has mastered his senses, the wise teacher should teach the knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the imperishable Person, the true, as it truly is. ॥1.2.13॥
1.2.iti: Thus ends the second khaṇḍa of the first Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
2.1.1: This is the truth: as from a fire burning bright sparks of its own form arise in their thousands, so, my dear, from the Imperishable beings of many kinds are born, and into it they return. ॥2.1.1॥
2.1.2: Divine and formless is that Person; he is without and within, unborn; without breath, without mind, pure, beyond even the Imperishable that is beyond all. ॥2.1.2॥
Śaṅkara takes the Imperishable here as the unmanifest, the seed of name and form, which is beyond all its effects; the Person is beyond even that.
2.1.3: From him are born prāṇa, mind and all the senses, space, air, fire, water, and the earth that holds up all. ॥2.1.3॥
2.1.4: Fire is his head, the moon and the sun his eyes, his ears the quarters, his speech the Vedas made known; air is his breath, the whole universe his heart; from his feet came the earth. He is the inner Self (ātman) of all beings. ॥2.1.4॥
Śaṅkara takes this as the cosmic form (virāṭ) born of that Person, and the fire here as heaven.
2.1.5: From him is the fire that has the sun for its fuel; from Soma, the rain cloud, and plants on the earth; a man pours his seed into a woman; so are many creatures born of the Person. ॥2.1.5॥
Śaṅkara takes this as the five fires: the fire is heaven, whose fuel is the sun; then the rain cloud, the earth, man and woman.
2.1.6: From him come the Ṛc verses, the Sāman chants, the Yajus formulas, initiation, all the sacrifices, the rites with a sacrificial post and the sacrificial fees, the year, the sacrificer and the worlds in which the moon purifies and the sun gives heat. ॥2.1.6॥
2.1.7: From him the gods were born in many forms, the Sādhyas, men, beasts and birds, the in-breath and the out-breath, rice and barley, tapas, faith, truth, continence and the rule of right conduct. ॥2.1.7॥
2.1.8: From him spring the seven prāṇas, the seven flames, the seven fuels, the seven oblations, and these seven worlds in which the prāṇas move; lying in the cave of the heart, they are placed there seven by seven. ॥2.1.8॥

Śaṅkara takes the seven prāṇas as the seven senses of the head (two eyes, two ears, two nostrils and the mouth); the flames are their power to light up their objects, the fuels their objects, the oblations their knowings and the worlds their seats.
2.1.9: All the seas and the mountains are from him; from him stream the rivers of every form. From him come all the plants and the sap by which this inner self (the subtle body) abides, surrounded by the elements. ॥2.1.9॥
2.1.10: All this universe, works and tapas, is the Person alone: Brahman, the supreme immortal. He who knows this, hidden in the cave of the heart, unties here, my dear, the knot of ignorance. ॥2.1.10॥
2.1.iti: Thus ends the first khaṇḍa of the second Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
2.2.1: Manifest, close at hand, known as the one who moves in the cave of the heart, is the great abode; in it all this is set: whatever moves, breathes and blinks. Know this, which is being and non-being, to be sought by all, the highest, beyond the knowing of creatures, the best of all. ॥2.2.1॥
Śaṅkara takes being and non-being as the gross and the subtle, the formed and the formless: it is both.
2.2.2: That which is luminous, which is subtler than the subtle, in which are set the worlds and those who dwell in them, that is this imperishable Brahman; that is prāṇa, that is speech and mind; that is the true, that is the immortal; that is the mark to be pierced, my dear: pierce it. ॥2.2.2॥
2.2.3: Taking up the bow, the great weapon taught in the Upaniṣads, one should set on it the arrow sharpened by meditation; drawing it with a mind absorbed in that, pierce, my dear, that very Imperishable, the mark. ॥2.2.3॥
2.2.4: The syllable Om is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its mark. It is to be pierced by one who is never careless; like the arrow, one should become one with it. ॥2.2.4॥
2.2.5: In whom heaven, earth and the space between are woven, and the mind with all the senses, know him alone, the one Self, and leave aside other words: this is the bridge to immortality. ॥2.2.5॥
2.2.6: Where the nāḍīs, the channels of the body, meet like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel, within it he moves, as though born in many ways. Meditate on the Self as Om. May it go well with you as you cross to the far shore beyond darkness. ॥2.2.6॥
2.2.7: He who is all-knowing and knows each thing, whose glory this is on earth: this Self is established in the space within the divine city of Brahman. He is made of mind, the leader of the breath and the body; having set the intellect in the heart, he abides in the body made of food. The wise behold him fully through knowledge, him who shines as bliss and as the immortal. ॥2.2.7॥
Śaṅkara takes the city of Brahman as the lotus of the heart, in whose space the Self is known, and hṛdayam in hṛdayaṃ sannidhāya as the intellect.
2.2.8: The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut away, and his works are spent, when he is seen who is both the higher and the lower. ॥2.2.8॥
2.2.9: In the highest golden sheath is Brahman, stainless and without parts; it is pure, the light of lights; it is what the knowers of the Self know. ॥2.2.9॥
2.2.10: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; nor do these lightnings shine; how then this fire? Everything shines after him alone, as he shines; by his light all this is lit. ॥2.2.10॥
2.2.11: What is in front is this immortal Brahman alone; Brahman is behind, Brahman to the south and to the north; it spreads out below and above; this universe is Brahman alone, the most excellent. ॥2.2.11॥
2.2.iti: Thus ends the second khaṇḍa of the second Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
3.1.1: Two birds of fair wings, ever united and friends, cling to the same tree. Of the two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit; the other, not eating, only looks on. ॥3.1.1॥
Śaṅkara takes the tree as the body, the two birds as the individual self and the Lord, and the fruit as the fruit of works.
3.1.2: Sunk in the same tree, the person grieves in his helplessness, bewildered. When he sees the other, the Lord whom the devout worship, and his greatness, he is freed from sorrow. ॥3.1.2॥
3.1.3: When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, Brahman the source of all, then the knower, shaking off merit and sin, stainless, attains the supreme sameness. ॥3.1.3॥
3.1.4: He who shines forth through all beings is indeed prāṇa. Knowing him, the wise one speaks of nothing beyond him. Sporting in the Self, delighting in the Self, active in spiritual practice, he is the foremost of the knowers of Brahman. ॥3.1.4॥
Śaṅkara takes prāṇa here as the Lord, the life of life itself.
3.1.5: This Self is to be attained by truth, by tapas, by right knowledge and by continence, practised always. Within the body, made of light and pure, is he whom the ascetics see, their faults worn away. ॥3.1.5॥
3.1.6: Truth alone prevails, not untruth. By truth is laid out the path of the gods, by which the seers, their desires fulfilled, ascend to where that supreme treasure of truth is. ॥3.1.6॥
3.1.7: It is vast, divine, of unthinkable form; subtler than the subtle, it shines. It is farther than the far, and it is here, near; in all beings that see, it is set right here, in the cave of the heart. ॥3.1.7॥
3.1.8: The eye does not grasp him, nor does speech, nor do the other senses, tapas or works. When the clarity of knowledge has made one pure in mind, then he sees him, who is without parts, as he meditates. ॥3.1.8॥
3.1.9: This subtle Self is to be known by the mind, where prāṇa has entered in five forms. The whole mind of creatures, together with the senses, is pervaded by that Self; when it is made pure, this Self shines forth. ॥3.1.9॥
Śaṅkara takes the place prāṇa has entered in five forms as the body: in that body, in the heart, the Self is to be known by the mind.
3.1.10: Whatever world the one of pure mind conceives in his mind, and whatever objects of desire he longs for, that world he wins, and those objects of desire. Therefore one who seeks prosperity should honour the knower of the Self. ॥3.1.10॥
3.1.iti: Thus ends the first khaṇḍa of the third Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
3.2.1: He knows this supreme Brahman, the abode in which the universe is set and which shines pure. The wise who, free of desire, worship that person pass beyond this seed of birth. ॥3.2.1॥
Śaṅkara takes this person as the knower of the Self of the mantra before, worshipped as the supreme God is; others take him as the supreme Person.
3.2.2: He who longs for objects of desire, dwelling on them, is born here and there because of those desires. But for one whose desires are fulfilled and whose self is perfected, all desires dissolve away even here. ॥3.2.2॥
3.2.3: This Self is not attained by discourse, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. It is attained by him alone whom it chooses; to him this Self reveals its own form. ॥3.2.3॥
Śaṅkara takes the chooser here as the seeker: the Self that the seeker chooses, longing for it alone, is attained by that very choosing and by no other means.
3.2.4: This Self is not attained by one who lacks strength, nor through heedlessness, nor by tapas without its mark. But the wise one who strives by these means, this Self of his enters the abode that is Brahman. ॥3.2.4॥
Śaṅkara takes the strength as that which comes of steadfastness in the Self, tapas here as knowledge, and its mark as renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
3.2.5: Having attained him, the seers, content with knowledge, their selves perfected, free from attachment and at peace, those wise ones, having reached the all-pervading on every side, with collected minds enter into the All itself. ॥3.2.5॥
3.2.6: Those who have well ascertained the meaning of the knowledge of the Vedānta, ascetics pure in mind through the discipline of renunciation, in the worlds of Brahman, at the time of the final end, one with the supreme immortal, are all wholly freed. ॥3.2.6॥

Śaṅkara takes the worlds of Brahman as Brahman itself, in the plural because many reach it, and the final end as the falling of the body; others take them as the worlds of Brahmā, from which they are freed at the end of the cosmic age.
3.2.7: The fifteen parts go back to their sources, and all the gods of the senses into their corresponding deities; his works and the self made of understanding all become one in the supreme, the imperishable. ॥3.2.7॥
Śaṅkara takes the fifteen parts as prāṇa and the others that make up the body, and the gods as those of the senses, which return to the sun and the other deities.
3.2.8: As flowing rivers, in the ocean, vanish, leaving name and form behind, so the knower, freed from name and form, reaches the divine Person, higher than the high. ॥3.2.8॥
3.2.9: He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his family no one is born who does not know Brahman. He crosses over sorrow, he crosses over sin; freed from the knots in the cave of the heart, he becomes immortal. ॥3.2.9॥
3.2.10: This is declared by a verse of the Veda: Those who perform the rites, are versed in the Veda and devoted to Brahman, who themselves offer oblations in the fire called Ekarṣi, full of faith, to them alone should one teach this knowledge of Brahman, by whom the vow of the head has been duly kept. ॥3.2.10॥
Śaṅkara takes Ekarṣi as the fire of that name, and the vow of the head as the Atharvavedins' well-known vow of carrying fire on the head.
3.2.11: This is the truth that the seer Aṅgiras told of old. One who has not kept the vow does not study it. Salutation to the supreme seers, salutation to the supreme seers. ॥3.2.11॥
3.2.iti: Thus ends the second khaṇḍa of the third Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.

shanti.1: Om. O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good; O you who are worthy of worship, may we see with our eyes what is good.
With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span of life the gods have set.
May Indra of great fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, who knows all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya, whose wheel no one can harm, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.
1.1.1: Om. Brahmā, the foremost of the gods, came into being, the maker of the universe
and the protector of the world. He taught the knowledge of Brahman (the Absolute), the ground of all knowledge, to Atharvan,
1.1.2: The knowledge that Brahmā taught to Atharvan,
that knowledge of Brahman Atharvan told of old to Aṅgir.
Aṅgir taught it to Satyavāha of the line of Bharadvāja,
and Satyavāha the Bhāradvāja taught it, handed down from teacher to pupil, to Aṅgiras. ॥1.1.2॥
1.1.3: Śaunaka, the great householder, having duly approached Aṅgiras, asked:
Venerable sir, what is it that, once known, makes all this known? ॥1.1.3॥
1.1.4: Two kinds of knowledge are to be known,
as the knowers of Brahman say: the higher and the lower. ॥1.1.4॥
1.1.5: Of these, the lower is the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda and the Atharvaveda,
phonetics, the ritual code, grammar, etymology, metre and astronomy.
And the higher is that by which the Imperishable (akṣara) is attained. ॥1.1.5॥
1.1.6: That which cannot be seen or grasped, which has no origin and no colour,
which has neither eyes nor ears, neither hands nor feet;
which is eternal, taking many forms, present everywhere and exceedingly subtle:
that is the Imperishable, which the wise see everywhere as the source of all beings. ॥1.1.6॥
1.1.7: As a spider sends out its thread and draws it in,
as plants spring up on the earth,
as hair of the head and body comes from a living man,
so here the universe arises from the Imperishable. ॥1.1.7॥
1.1.8: Through tapas (heat, austerity) Brahman swells; from it food is born.
From food come prāṇa (the life-breath), mind, the true and the worlds, and in works the immortal (their fruit). ॥1.1.8॥
1.1.9: He who is all-knowing and knows each thing, whose tapas is made of knowledge:
from him are born this Brahman, name, form and food. ॥1.1.9॥
1.1.iti: Thus ends the first khaṇḍa (section) of the first Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.

2.1.1: as from a fire burning bright
sparks of its own form arise in their thousands,
so, my dear, from the Imperishable beings of many kinds
are born, and into it they return. ॥2.1.1॥
2.1.2: Divine and formless is that Person; he is without and within, unborn;
without breath, without mind, pure, beyond even the Imperishable that is beyond all. ॥2.1.2॥
2.1.3: From him are born prāṇa, mind and all the senses,
space, air, fire, water, and the earth that holds up all. ॥2.1.3॥
2.1.4: Fire is his head, the moon and the sun his eyes,
his ears the quarters, his speech the Vedas made known;
air is his breath, the whole universe his heart; from his feet
came the earth. He is the inner Self (ātman) of all beings. ॥2.1.4॥
2.1.5: From him is the fire that has the sun for its fuel;
from Soma, the rain cloud, and plants on the earth;
a man pours his seed into a woman;
so are many creatures born of the Person. ॥2.1.5॥
2.1.6: From him come the Ṛc verses, the Sāman chants, the Yajus formulas, initiation,
all the sacrifices, the rites with a sacrificial post and the sacrificial fees,
the year, the sacrificer and the worlds
in which the moon purifies and the sun gives heat. ॥2.1.6॥
2.1.7: From him the gods were born in many forms,
the Sādhyas, men, beasts and birds,
the in-breath and the out-breath, rice and barley, tapas,
faith, truth, continence and the rule of right conduct. ॥2.1.7॥
2.1.8: From him spring the seven prāṇas,
the seven flames, the seven fuels, the seven oblations,
and these seven worlds in which the prāṇas move;
lying in the cave of the heart, they are placed there seven by seven. ॥2.1.8॥
2.1.9: All the seas and the mountains are from him; from him
stream the rivers of every form.
From him come all the plants and the sap
by which this inner self (the subtle body) abides, surrounded by the elements. ॥2.1.9॥
2.1.10: All this universe, works and tapas, is the Person alone: Brahman, the supreme immortal.
He who knows this, hidden in the cave of the heart,
unties here, my dear, the knot of ignorance. ॥2.1.10॥
2.1.iti: Thus ends the first khaṇḍa of the second Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
2.2.1: Manifest, close at hand, known as the one who moves in the cave of the heart,
is the great abode; in it all this is set:
whatever moves, breathes and blinks. Know this, which is
being and non-being, to be sought by all, the highest, beyond the knowing of creatures, the best of all. ॥2.2.1॥
2.2.2: That which is luminous, which is subtler than the subtle,
in which are set the worlds and those who dwell in them,
that is this imperishable Brahman; that is prāṇa, that is speech and mind;
that is the true, that is the immortal; that is the mark to be pierced, my dear: pierce it. ॥2.2.2॥
2.2.3: Taking up the bow, the great weapon taught in the Upaniṣads,
one should set on it the arrow sharpened by meditation;
drawing it with a mind absorbed in that,
pierce, my dear, that very Imperishable, the mark. ॥2.2.3॥
2.2.4: The syllable Om is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its mark.
It is to be pierced by one who is never careless; like the arrow, one should become one with it. ॥2.2.4॥
2.2.5: In whom heaven, earth and the space between are woven,
and the mind with all the senses,
know him alone, the one Self, and leave aside
other words: this is the bridge to immortality. ॥2.2.5॥
2.2.6: Where the nāḍīs, the channels of the body, meet like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel,
within it he moves, as though born in many ways.
Meditate on the Self as Om. May it go well with you
as you cross to the far shore beyond darkness. ॥2.2.6॥
2.2.7: He who is all-knowing and knows each thing, whose glory this is on earth:
this Self is established in the space within the divine city of Brahman.
He is made of mind, the leader of the breath and the body;
having set the intellect in the heart, he abides in the body made of food.
The wise behold him fully through knowledge,
him who shines as bliss and as the immortal. ॥2.2.7॥
2.2.8: The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut away,
and his works are spent, when he is seen who is both the higher and the lower. ॥2.2.8॥
2.2.9: In the highest golden sheath is Brahman, stainless and without parts;
it is pure, the light of lights; it is what the knowers of the Self know. ॥2.2.9॥
2.2.10: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars;
nor do these lightnings shine; how then this fire?
Everything shines after him alone, as he shines;
by his light all this is lit. ॥2.2.10॥
2.2.11: What is in front is this immortal Brahman alone; Brahman is behind, Brahman to the south and to the north;
it spreads out below and above; this universe is Brahman alone, the most excellent. ॥2.2.11॥
2.2.iti: Thus ends the second khaṇḍa of the second Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
3.1.1: Two birds of fair wings, ever united and friends, cling to the same tree.
Of the two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit; the other, not eating, only looks on. ॥3.1.1॥
3.1.2: Sunk in the same tree, the person grieves in his helplessness, bewildered.
When he sees the other, the Lord whom the devout worship,
and his greatness, he is freed from sorrow. ॥3.1.2॥
3.1.3: When the seer sees the golden-hued one,
the maker, the Lord, the Person, Brahman the source of all,
then the knower, shaking off merit and sin,
3.1.4: He who shines forth through all beings is indeed prāṇa.
Knowing him, the wise one speaks of nothing beyond him.
Sporting in the Self, delighting in the Self, active in spiritual practice,
he is the foremost of the knowers of Brahman. ॥3.1.4॥
3.1.5: This Self is to be attained by truth, by tapas,
by right knowledge and by continence, practised always.
Within the body, made of light and pure, is he
whom the ascetics see, their faults worn away. ॥3.1.5॥
3.1.6: By truth is laid out the path of the gods,
by which the seers, their desires fulfilled, ascend
to where that supreme treasure of truth is. ॥3.1.6॥
3.1.7: It is vast, divine, of unthinkable form;
subtler than the subtle, it shines.
It is farther than the far, and it is here, near;
in all beings that see, it is set right here, in the cave of the heart. ॥3.1.7॥
3.1.8: The eye does not grasp him, nor does speech,
nor do the other senses, tapas or works.
When the clarity of knowledge has made one pure in mind,
then he sees him, who is without parts,
3.1.9: This subtle Self is to be known by the mind,
where prāṇa has entered in five forms.
The whole mind of creatures, together with the senses, is pervaded by that Self;
when it is made pure, this Self shines forth. ॥3.1.9॥
3.1.10: Whatever world the one of pure mind conceives in his mind,
and whatever objects of desire he longs for,
that world he wins, and those objects of desire.
Therefore one who seeks prosperity should honour the knower of the Self. ॥3.1.10॥
3.1.iti: Thus ends the first khaṇḍa of the third Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
3.2.1: He knows this supreme Brahman, the abode
in which the universe is set and which shines pure.
The wise who, free of desire, worship that person
pass beyond this seed of birth. ॥3.2.1॥
3.2.2: He who longs for objects of desire, dwelling on them,
is born here and there because of those desires.
But for one whose desires are fulfilled and whose self is perfected,
all desires dissolve away even here. ॥3.2.2॥
3.2.3: This Self is not attained by discourse,
nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
It is attained by him alone whom it chooses;
to him this Self reveals its own form. ॥3.2.3॥
3.2.4: This Self is not attained by one who lacks strength,
nor through heedlessness, nor by tapas without its mark.
But the wise one who strives by these means,
this Self of his enters the abode that is Brahman. ॥3.2.4॥
3.2.5: Having attained him, the seers, content with knowledge,
their selves perfected, free from attachment and at peace,
those wise ones, having reached the all-pervading on every side,
with collected minds enter into the All itself. ॥3.2.5॥
3.2.6: Those who have well ascertained the meaning of the knowledge of the Vedānta,
ascetics pure in mind through the discipline of renunciation,
in the worlds of Brahman, at the time of the final end,
one with the supreme immortal, are all wholly freed. ॥3.2.6॥
3.2.7: The fifteen parts go back to their sources,
and all the gods of the senses into their corresponding deities;
his works and the self made of understanding
all become one in the supreme, the imperishable. ॥3.2.7॥
3.2.8: As flowing rivers, in the ocean,
vanish, leaving name and form behind,
so the knower, freed from name and form,
reaches the divine Person, higher than the high. ॥3.2.8॥
3.2.9: He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman
becomes Brahman itself; in his family no one is born who does not know Brahman.
He crosses over sorrow, he crosses over sin; freed from the knots in the cave of the heart,
3.2.10: This is declared by a verse of the Veda:
Those who perform the rites, are versed in the Veda and devoted to Brahman,
who themselves offer oblations in the fire called Ekarṣi, full of faith,
to them alone should one teach this knowledge of Brahman,
by whom the vow of the head has been duly kept. ॥3.2.10॥
3.2.11: This is the truth that the seer Aṅgiras
told of old. One who has not kept the vow does not study it.
Salutation to the supreme seers, salutation to the supreme seers. ॥3.2.11॥
3.2.iti: Thus ends the second khaṇḍa of the third Muṇḍaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
